## Project idea

For my final project, I plan to study how visitation at U.S. national parks
has changed over time and how seasonal patterns differ from park to park. I
assembled three NPS annual visitation reports into one dataset covering
1979–2025, with 16,095 park-year observations. The separate 2025 ranking
report adds each park's rank and share of total visits.

The variables I am most interested in are **park name**, **year**, and
**recreation visits**. I will use them to compare parks and explore long-term
changes in popularity. The annual report also includes other visitor-use
statistics, such as visitor hours and overnight stays, which could help me
compare different kinds of park use.

## Which park was most visited each year?

Each small gray dot is one park's annual recreation visits. The red dots
highlight the most-visited park in each year, and the red line connects those
annual leaders. The pseudo-log scale keeps the many smaller parks visible
alongside parks with millions of visits.

```{r}
#| label: fig-park-visitation-dots
#| fig-cap: "Annual recreation visits for every park-year; red marks the most-visited park in each year."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

library(tidyverse)

annual_visits <- read_csv(
  "nps_annual_visits_1979_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

annual_leaders <- annual_visits |>
  group_by(year) |>
  slice_max(recreation_visits, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(annual_visits, aes(x = year, y = recreation_visits)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.18, height = 0, seed = 2026),
    color = "#52738A",
    alpha = 0.18,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = annual_leaders,
    aes(group = 1),
    color = "#C64F3D",
    linewidth = 0.9,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = annual_leaders,
    color = "#C64F3D",
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = filter(annual_leaders, year == max(year)),
    aes(label = park),
    nudge_x = 1,
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3,
    color = "#8E3328",
    fill = "white",
    label.size = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1980, 2025, by = 5),
    limits = c(1979, 2034)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    trans = scales::transform_pseudo_log(sigma = 1),
    breaks = c(0, 100000, 1000000, 5000000, 10000000, 20000000),
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The most-visited park in each year",
    subtitle = "Every dot is a park-year observation, 1979–2025",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Annual recreation visits (pseudo-log scale)",
    caption = paste0(
      format(nrow(annual_visits), big.mark = ","),
      " park-year dots; red dots and line show each year's leader. ",
      "Reporting park counts vary by year. Source: NPS annual visitation reports."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#17324D", size = 20),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#526477"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#667085", hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

## Questions I hope to explore

- Which parks have the most recreation visits, and how has that changed over
  time? This plot focuses on annual recreation visits and highlights the
  leading park in each year.
- Which months tend to be busiest or quietest, and which parks have the
  strongest seasonal swings? My current CSV files are annual, so I need
  monthly data to answer this part.
- Did visitation patterns shift in particular years? Monthly data could show
  month-by-month changes, but would not identify visits on specific holidays.

## Data sources

- [NPS Visitor Use Statistics portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/)
- [NPS Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm)

The NPS dashboard describes the monthly series as beginning in 1979 and
provides park-level and monthly or annual views. I will check the data
definitions and limitations before interpreting comparisons.

To study seasonal patterns, I should download a **monthly park-level
visitation report** from the NPS portal, with park name or code, year, month,
and recreation visits. Ideally it would cover 1979 through the most recent
complete year. Monthly data can answer which months are busiest, but
holiday-specific analysis would require daily visitation data, if available.

The annual reports cover up to 20 years each, so I combined report periods
1979–1998, 1999–2018, and 2019–2025 for the full historical view. The number
of reporting park units changes over time, so comparisons describe the
distribution among units reporting in each year.
